This paper proposes a novel approach for object detection, referred to as BayesOD. This method utilizes the Bayesian two-stage object detection transformer (TOD) to generate an uncertainty estimate for each prediction, including the location, size, and category confidence of the detected object. By integrating an uncertainty loss into the training process, BayesOD achieves a significant improvement of 1.5 times in estimating object category uncertainty, in comparison to using the TDD's average prediction confidence, while maintaining predictive accuracy without compromise. Furthermore, BayesOD offers a substantial advantage of 1.5 times in estimating spatial uncertainty for the object's location, while also achieving a significant enhancement of 40% for size uncertainty, when compared to the method of predicting a single class probability map for each object class. The performance of BayesOD is evaluated across a range of datasets, including COCO, ADE20k, Cityscapes, MakePD, and PASCAL-VOC, demonstrating a superior outcome over the current state-of-the-art in object detection uncertainty estimation. The code for BayesOD is available at https://github.com/ashwini11111111/bayesOD.

Traffic forecasting, a crucial component of traffic analysis, is being revolutionized by a particular neural network approach, with various innovative solutions emerging to tackle the challenge. Recent advancements in deep learning have further accelerated the development of cutting-edge traffic forecasting systems. In contrast to traditional deep learning-based methods, the proposed Trama-fc model leverages an enhanced Unet++ architecture, outperforming the former in multiple aspects, including its ability to retain and interpret detailed information, while also showcasing robust models, robustness to dataset variations, and robustness in comparison to state-of-the-art Unet++ based Trama-fc model, the proposed Trama-fc achieves superior performance in various benchmarks, including a single-city dataset, multi-city dataset and real-world dataset, the latter of which the model, the minimum improvement over the Unet++ based Trama-fc achieves over 1% in multiple datasets, the proposed Trama-fc achieves over 1% in multiple datasets, while the Unet++ based Trama-fc achieves over 1% in multiple datasets.

The existing definition of weak categories, which are precategories equipped with a coherent rewriting system having a single terminal object, is shown to be ineffectively cumbersome in practice. In an effort to simplify this definition, weak categories are redefined as precategories equipped with a coherent weak structure, comprising two distinct systems: one governing identity morphisms and the other governing composition of morphisms. We demonstrate that this revised definition remains equivalent to the conventional one, yet offers a more practical approach. Additionally, the process of strictening weak categories, previously explored in relation to strict category semantics, is contextualised within these new insights, yielding a fresh understanding of the connection between strict categories and strict categories with a coherent weak structure.

A developed automated hippocampus segmentation tool, claimed to perform well on unaltered hippocampi, is evaluated to determine its reliability on altered hippocampi post-hippocampus resection for epilepsy, which may have implications for post-surgery memory assessment. Using T2-weighted MRI scans from 40 epilepsy patients who underwent resection and 40 healthy controls, evaluation metrics were used to assess accuracy, compatibility, and localization of the method across various resection sites. Results showed that the method's accuracy for healthy controls matches its original performance, but for resection cases, the method's accuracy declined significantly, most notably around the resection site. Overall, the results suggest that the method generally accurately segments the remaining hippocampus tissue away from the resection site but becomes inaccurate near the resection site.

Quantum experiments are becoming more complex, spanning from circuit to field theories, and often assume that light's movement has no effect. This assumption is not always the case, and a simple, four-source light model is used to show how light's path and FREDHOFF-WILKSON ZUMANOSKY degrees of freedom are connected. This model can be easily performed in any lab setting, is based on widely accepted principles, and demonstrates the connection between these concepts. Building upon this knowledge, the model is expanded to incorporate the effect of light's movement and polarization, providing a new understanding of high-dimensional light systems.

When high-energy cosmic rays strike the Earth's atmosphere, they generate protons through a series of collisions that can initiate the development of an extensive air shower. The interaction between the incoming particles and nitrogen nuclei at the top of the atmosphere has a mean free path of a few meters, limiting the depth at which the first hadronic interaction occurs. As a result, any changes in the flux of incoming cosmic rays are attenuated before reaching the Earth's surface, necessitating a correction factor when interpreting data from measurements of the isotropic muon flux to infer variations in the primary flux. To address this issue, a numerical model of the atmosphere has been created, simulating the propagation of high-energy cosmic rays and their associated hadronic interactions that ultimately produce the isotropic muon flux detected at the Earth's surface. This model can account for changes in the primary flux to determine the corresponding variations in the isotropic muon flux detected by experiments such as A4, which is currently involved in a worldwide collaboration to determine the all-energy isotropic muon flux.

A neural network's performance is heavily reliant on the effectiveness of its training. During this process, gradients are passed backward through time, ultimately influencing the weights of early layers. Unfortunately, the hierarchical structure of traditional neural networks hampers this training efficiency, resulting in slower convergence and potential loss of information. To overcome this limitation, we have developed a novel pyramidal skeleton architecture, which optimizes the training trajectory by enabling the later layers to converge faster and significantly enhancing the training efficiency. Furthermore, the architecture's hierarchical structure facilitates efficient information aggregation and reduces the architecture's depth, thereby accelerating inference. We have successfully applied this framework to create different neural network models, all of which have been thoroughly tested and have been shown to excel in various tasks. Specifically, the new models surpass or match existing benchmarks on important datasets like ImageNet, StreetView, and ADE20k, consistently delivering state-of-the-art results.

This paper investigates the application of sensitive mechanisms within differential private learning methods. A proposed mechanism outperforms established methods like Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms in numerical prediction tasks. Our work introduces and analyzes four novel mechanisms - Huber, Huber2, exponential, and exponential2 - modifications to existing mechanisms inspired by the Huber outlier suppression technique for statistical estimation. A performance assessment in differential private learning tasks for non-sensitive data releases reveals that our novel mechanisms achieve better results than the conventional ones. For instance, in Gaussian data, a Huber-based mechanism excels over the Laplace-based mechanism when the given sensitivity is smaller than the chosen threshold. We further demonstrate that differential private mechanisms developed for specific types of data, such as binary and multinomial data, can achieve better results than conventional mechanisms when an appropriate threshold is chosen appropriately.

The presence of interstellar dust is evident through its absorption of light and emission of heat in the near-infrared to far-infrared spectrum. Observations of dust polarization provide insight into its shape, alignment with magnetic fields, and intrinsic polarization properties. We studied the far-infrared polarization of 11 stars using the Herschel/PHOTOP project and found that the polarization fraction increased with the extinction of light, following a consistent, linear relationship. Interestingly, the infrared polarized emission from the dust did not show any variation with frequency, which was observed in 9 of the stars studied. We hypothesized that the absence of variation could be due to the presence of large, interstellar dust grains, specifically "pebbles," that have shaped themselves in the inner regions of star formation and then fragmented. The uniform shape of the larger grains and regular alignment with magnetic fields could have led to a uniform, linear relationship in the polarization and an absence of variation with frequency in the dust's emitted light. The uniformity of the larger grains may also explain the observed uniformity of the infrared polarized emission.

The protoplanetary disk surrounding PDS 2222 is currently undergoing a phase where massive planets are forming a dust ring at a particular distance from the central star. This observation aligns with predictions of how a massive planet would impact the central emission of the disk, causing the central area to appear empty in certain wavelengths due to the disk's warping effect. This theory suggests that the gas observed in recent studies, emitted at a steeper angle than the dust in outer regions, could be explained by the presence of a massive planet influencing the central disk structure. This theory is consistent with the discovered 100 au dust ring and a 0.16 arcsec point source located within the central area. This point source is consistent with the predicted location of the planet responsible for the observed ring structure, and its estimated mass is around 3 Jupiter masses. This mass is consistent with estimates derived from dynamical considerations, independent of the ring structure. This theory is also consistent with observations of gas kinematics, suggesting that the inner regions of the disk are being influenced by the massive planet, causing the central areas to be illuminated at a steeper angle than the outer regions. The Most Clicks Problem, or MCP, is a crucial challenge within Facebook's advertising system. It involves finding the best click matrix of a given size, defined by its dimensions $m \times n$, with a value of either 0 or 1 in each cell, maximizing the total occurrences of the number 1. A key observation is that these occurrences correspond to the rank-deficiency of submatrices, and this rank-deficiency can be expressed as the smallest $k$ such that matrices of size $(m-k) \times (n-k)$ achieve full rank, with all possible configurations. By focusing on these matrices, we can establish a direct link to the study of unimodular matrices and develop new methods for approximating the lower bound of the optimal solution. Our main contribution in this study is the introduction of an innovative algorithm that accurately computes the optimal solution for any given pair of $m \times n$.

The Wilson et al. model, derived from the piecewise constant Mumford-Shah model, effectively segments corrupted images by incorporating a data fidelity term. A novel Wilson et al. variant for hypergraphs is developed, utilizing a new coefficient to regulate noise impact. This new model's complexity is reduced through optimization, utilizing a linear operator formulation of the total variation term. The corresponding Euler-Lagrange equations are established, leading to a dual-domain system of equations. A preconditioned conjugate gradient method is employed to efficiently solve this system, which is further accelerated using a conjugate gradient algorithm in the dual space. Experimental results, conducted on both synthetic and real images, demonstrate the proposed model, PHW, outperforms the previous HW model, as well as other image segmentation techniques, including graph-cut, in terms of accuracy and efficiency. Notably, PhW significantly improves over HW, achieving an average increase of 6.2% in precision and recall rates. Moreover, PHw exhibits superior performance on various color images and color text, completing tasks 1.5 times faster than HW.

The path-coverage criterion, introduced by Gulwani and Wilcox, offers strong guarantees for abstract interpolation, including path coverage, invariant inversion, and termination. However, computing this criterion can be costly, as it requires the flow of control information to be fully tracked, compromising efficiency. To strike a balance between performance and theoretical assurances, we propose a method that enables partial flow of control information to be followed, thus improving abstract interpolation's efficiency. Our method offers an approximate criterion, as it skips following control path branches deemed unlikely, based on prior abstract exploration. Our implementation shows that this approximation leads to substantial speedups of up to 1000x. The approach is open-source, hosted on GitHub at https://github.com/facebook/faip.

Tetragonal perovskite phases, in their ground state, exhibit different structural phases separated by quantum mechanical transitions. This work demonstrates how photoexcitation, an environmentally controllable method, can efficiently trigger these transitions, leading to the formation of a topologically complex phononic structure. Photoexcitation, controlled by light intensity, can both eliminate gapping in these structures and induce a topological transition, leading to the emergence of non-Planckian phononic band gaps. These bands exhibit a high phonon density and can be manipulated through photoexcitation, leading the system into a topologically complex phononic crystal state. In this topologically complex state, the system exhibits a partial band gap, characterized by the presence of edge phonon modes. This research provides a technique for creating and controlling topologically complex phononic crystals, potentially paving the way for the creation of efficient phononic devices.

The detection of outliers in large movement track data sets through semantic proximity is an underexplored topic. The application of Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) proximity graphs to this scope presents challenges, particularly in terms of scalability and efficiency. This study introduces the concept of a Modified Randomized Proximity Graph (MRPG), tailored for processing large movement track data sets. By initially eliminating outliers and then focusing on tracking in the remaining data, MRPG efficiently balances preprocessing and tracking performance. The proposed MST approximation algorithm leverages the track structure, enabling it to operate on significantly smaller Randomized Proximity Graphs and substantially improving efficiency. Computational experiments demonstrate that MRPG outperforms existing methods, achieving substantial reductions in near-neighbors computation time and outlier detection rates. Additionally, MST approximation offers a 100-fold speedup over random approaches. Overall, the proposed MRPG framework effectively addresses proximity graph construction and outlier detection in large movement track data sets, providing a scalable solution for tracking applications.

A long-standing debate exists about whether an atom in motion always emits a photon, even if it's electrically neutral. Our study tackles this question by examining a mobile dipole attached to a planar mirror and deriving a quantum Langevin equation for the atom-mirror system. The effect of the vacuum and thermal fields on the atom is analyzed by calculating a frequency-dependent polarizability, which depends on both the motion and the temperature. Our analysis reveals that an atom with a constant velocity below a certain speed limit can remain dark, even if the atom-mirror system introduces two separate emitters. Our study reveals that below a certain speed limit, a dipole that's normally a perfect blackbody radiator becomes imperceptible. Our investigation also reveals that friction arises from a change in the force exerted by the Casimir interaction on the atom-mirror system in response to disturbances. Our study provides valuable insights into the connection between atomic emitters, the Casimir effect, and atomic trampoline technology.

Deep learning graph models excel at translating graph structures into machine-readable representations. In numerous applications, achieving community or node-level fairness is essential, prompting researchers to focus on developing representations that conform to these fairness principles. However, the impact of enforcing fairness in network representation learning has not been thoroughly examined. This study investigates how incorporating fairness into learning processes affects representation accuracy and fairness, both in terms of individual nodes and fair subgraphs. We provide a theoretical framework for understanding the trade-offs between fairness and accuracy, and support our findings with a comprehensive experimental analysis. The results highlight the importance of selecting the right fairness approach, which should be informed by the specific fairness criteria needed and the underlying data and model choices.

The research compares the application of Homotopy Perturbation Method (HPM) and Simple Iteration Method (SIM) in modeling enzymatic reaction systems. Focusing on enzyme reversibility, this study derives equations using SIM and hlm and evaluates their approximations relative to HPM and SIM approximations when a large value of k_es is considered. This comparison reveals that while both methods yield similar outcomes, the hlm method introduces an additional parameter enhancing its ability to capture system behavior. By normalizing equations, this study introduces a new approach to HPM, extending its applicability and enabling estimation of initial system conditions.

A long-lived gluino with a mass of at least 2.1 TeV, which decays into hadrons, is sought after at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) with an innovative strategy. By extending the existing hadronic decay search to a greater sensitivity of decay variations, this novel approach offers the capacity to uncover gluinos with decay lengths up to 300 cm. Unlike conventional searches, this method demonstrates equal capability in detecting gluinos with decay lengths as short as 1 cm, thereby encompassing a broader spectrum of possibilities. Furthermore, the intersection of the excluded gluino parameter space with that anticipated by the LHC's conventional search reveals the potential discovery of gluinos with masses ranging from 2 to 2.3 TeV, which, when combined with a half-life of approximately 30 microseconds, can also be compared to limits set by the LHC's conventional search.

Financial markets often experience dramatic and unpredictable price swings, which can lead to the rapid escalation of asset bubbles followed by their sudden collapse, causing significant losses for investors. This study explores the underlying reasons for these phenomena, focusing on how individual investors' behavior, such as their tendency to imitate one another, affects bubble formation and cessation. It is discovered that negative feedback resulting from imitation first causes bubbles to stabilize, oscillating around fair prices with varying magnitudes, which diminish over time as the negative feedback weakens. Conversely, strong imitation drives all bubbles to ultimately collapse, which can be attributed to the emergence of a Hopf bifurcation point at a specific value of the feedback strength. Furthermore, it is observed that sudden, unexpected events can unexpectedly halt accelerating bubbles, which in turn leads to the emergence of volatile and turbulent prices, which can be identified through fractal patterns and low-dimensional chaotic dynamics.

The method of integrating out in finite systems has been successfully utilized to identify effective Hamiltonians, which can extend quasiclassical descriptions beyond quasiclassical drive conditions. It has been found that in driven systems a target described by a coherent state is always achievable, represented by an infinite-dimensional pendulum with a shifted and rotated axis of stable equilibrium. A weak infinite-dimensional harmonic oscillator emerges within this revised model, enabling the derivation of improved pendulum-based quasiclassical descriptions outside quasiclassical drive regimes.

A data-driven recommendation approach that incorporates review interactions from a community of reviewers is proposed. By integrating review activity in real-time, this model can more accurately predict final ratings. It is implemented within an existing e-commerce platform and demonstrates improved performance using a results set of 50K users and 1.3M review events. The feature engineering process is adaptable to various applications.

This paper addresses the scarcity of training data for segmentally code-switched speech synthesis, a task often neglected in existing multilingual speech synthesis approaches. To overcome this challenge, a neural approach was developed, drawing inspiration from previous work in word-level code-switching, but this time applied to segments such as phonemes or character nemoings. A dataset created through human transcription and segmentation was evaluated, showing improved accuracy over previous full translation-based methods. Additionally, automatic estimation of the code-switching pattern was demonstrated, facilitating the training of a neural decoder without ground truth information. Ultimately, the paper presents a simple neural model utilizing attention, and this method's effectiveness is thoroughly examined through a case study in this research.

Consider a compact surface, denoted as X, equipped with its interior X°. An action of a subgroup H of a lattice Γ < Isom(X) is examined. When H is a subgroup of a transitive Γ₁ on X°, it performs a precompact action. Furthermore, if H is a subgroup of Γ₁ on X°, it indeed generates a precompact action. Ultimately, all possible H subgroup configurations under Γ's action are fully classified.

Two types of five-dimensional conical brane geometries that meet at a specific radius are identified and classified. These geometries, which solve the equations for scalar fields in a 5D space with a conical singularity, can in principle resolve such singularities. The proposed models demonstrate the behavior of these branes in a specific gravitational context that transitions between different stages. The first stage features a 4D space with a cosmological constant, while the second stage features a 4D space with a different cosmological constant. The investigation reveals that the transition can occur in both directions and that the resulting singularity is a potential big-bang singularity in some cases. The findings also highlight potential challenges and difficulties in implementing these models.

The quality of a mesh's building blocks, such as triangles and tetrahedra, impacts the overall reliability of computational methods.  When high-quality meshes are used, algorithms often produce accurate results, but low-quality elements can lead to incorrect outcomes.  As simulations become more complex, algorithms more advanced, and meshes more detailed, the need for automatic mesh generation becomes increasingly crucial.  This process involves adjusting generation parameters or modifying initial meshes to ensure all elements meet a minimum standard.  This paper outlines a framework for automatic mesh improvement, focusing on identifying low-quality elements, removing them, and replacing them with functional versions.  This framework is adaptable to various types of elements and can be applied to different mesh types, including polyhedra.  A separate section discusses how to remove vertices that hinder simulation performance due to poor element quality.  A separate section introduces heuristics that enhance the overall mesh structure, including tetrahedra sharing more than one vertex.  A separate section demonstrates the application of this framework and associated methods on a sample mesh, including high-quality and low-quality elements.  A separate section discusses the implications of mesh optimization, including its impact on accuracy and performance.  A separate section discusses the limitations of this framework and presents potential areas for further research.

This paper examines two key tasks in graph representation learning: knowledge graph link prediction and relation extraction. The focus is on understanding how these tasks can be connected and if they can be effectively addressed jointly. Specifically, we explore the link between these tasks and compare existing approaches to relation extraction with the potential for leveraging additional prediction tasks through semi-supervised or multi-task learning. Ultimately, we propose a novel framework for jointly performing link prediction and relation extraction, which is evaluated in an experiment on open data. The results indicate that this proposed method outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches on both related tasks.

This paper introduces a novel architecture for high-performance, energy-efficient, and scalable analog computing systems that can process complex mathematical functions without relying on digital hardware or software assistance. A comprehensive delay model is developed for the proposed architecture and can be integrated into circuit simulation tools with ease. A key feature of this model is its ability to accurately predict transmission delays with minimal error, as demonstrated through SPICE simulations of various waveforms. Notably, the model achieves a percentage error of less than 1% for transmission delays and less than 1.1% for switching times. Furthermore, the integration of the new architecture resulted in a 2.76x reduction in static power consumption and a 2.44x decrease in transmission delay compared to the implemented circuit.

This paper presents an innovative coarse-grained function approximation method, using smoothness to learn better control policies in continuous state-action environments. Building on a new coreset-inspired technique, our approach selects an efficient set of states for PILCO learning, improving samples per iteration and production deployment. By incorporating control-path smoothness and state-cover efficiency, our method dynamically adjusts PILCO iterations and hyperparameters. Experimental comparisons show our method outperforms baseline coresets consistently, routinely, and significantly.

Our comprehension of the concept "living" is significantly aided by grouping entities into distinct categories. This research explores the role of these categories versus individual examples in shaping our mental framework for what it means to be "living." Through a novel method that uses visual categorizability and cognitive categorization to measure our perceptions of "living things," we employed two distinct approaches to categorize entities: one based on visual characteristics and another grounded in conceptual understanding. The outcomes of these experiments show that our categorization of "living things" is influenced more by our cognitive framework than by our ability to categorize entities based on their visual characteristics. Furthermore, our findings suggest that our concept of "living things" is influenced by our capacity to recognize ourselves and others as agents, but not by our capacity to categorize entities based on their visual characteristics. Our study contributes to both cognitive science and AI by offering valuable insights and new tools for understanding the concept of "living things."

Data assimilation methodologies have been developed to maintain certain properties in partial differential equation models. A new approach has been proposed that utilizes graph neural networks in a non-linear filter. This method is particularly effective for quadratic invariants but can also be extended to handle higher-order invariants. The approach addresses issues with inconsistencies in polynomial-based PDE simulations and is data- and hyperparameter-driven. Through various 1D and 2D examples, the proposed method demonstrates a range of impressive performance improvements, surpassing existing data assimilation methods.

We conducted an observational study of the black hole X-ray binary, H1725-299, by using 2-ms timing data from XIS on ISXTS, specifically focusing on its first outburst in 2018. A notable feature of the black hole X-ray binary's light curve, during specific phases of its spectral state transitions, is the presence of quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs). We observed two distinct types of QPOs, referred to as "type-C" and "type-B", occurring in different sections of the spectral state diagram. The type-C QPO frequency exhibited an increase in correlation with fractional hard X-ray flux by approximately 0.1 Hz per 0.1 increase in fractional hard X-ray flux. Furthermore, the type-B QPO frequency was observed to correlate positively with fractional hard X-ray flux by approximately 0.05 Hz per 0.1 increase in fractional hard X-ray flux, consistent with previous research. The type-B QPO amplitude was observed to correlate positively with fractional hard X-ray flux by approximately 0.02, indicating a significant increase in its amplitude.

A key challenge in multi-agent reinforcement learning arises from the limited sample efficiency and learning stability that are required when learning each agent's policy within a collaborative goal-oriented environment. In this paper, a new empowerment empowerment learning framework, based on the transfer empowerment learning approach, is developed to address this issue. The sample efficiency and learning stability that are promoted by the transfer empowerment learning approach are further augmented through the shared empirical distribution that is learned and shared among agents. The empirical distribution that is represented by a histogram and reflects agent-observation pairs plays a pivotal role in improving performance. The learning framework's novel aspects involve leveraging only joint-observation states for the learning of a shared empirical distribution and the incorporation of a Kullback-Leibler divergence-based regularization that complements the learning of a shared empirical distribution. The effectiveness of this approach is substantiated through experimental results that demonstrate its superiority over state-of-the-art algorithms in multiple reward and multiple goal-oriented tasks, including multi-room agent communication and agent cooperation within agent-swarm.

Our method leverages recent advancements in one-shot learning, specifically those based on Siamese networks, to identify the material of an object under varying environmental conditions, object angles, and lighting. To accommodate different scenarios such as underwater or indoor settings, we adapted the one-shot material recognition task to operate using image features extracted by a CNN from input data, and further modified it to process features from a Siamese network that learns material characteristics under varying conditions. To train the system, we created the MatriMat dataset, which captures images of 22 distinct materials from multiple angles and across different environments. Our novel approach achieved successful results on this new benchmark, using either a single shot or composite images of one or two shots to recognize materials in unfamiliar scenarios.

Using cohomology, we reframe Lie 2-algebra cohomology, specifically focusing on its lower-dimensional aspects which maintain universal significance. This reframe offers a clear cohomological interpretation for key 2-algebra concepts such as scalar, vector, and scalar curvature, as well as their associated connections. Additionally, we demonstrate the cohomology's applicability in the context of group cohomology.

Conventional methods rely on image feature detection and matching, but they suffer
from issues such as low efficiency and inaccuracies. A novel approach is presented
for multi-view 3D reconstruction by learning 2D-3D correspondences, using features
that effectively convey view relationships. Instead of traditional features, this
method learns multi-scale features with a unique view association capability. 3D points
are regressed directly using encoded image encoding, avoiding the limitations of existing
 approaches. This proposed method demonstrates significant improvements on shape reconstruction
 benchmarks, showcasing its effectiveness through ablation studies.

The accuracy of automated vector magnetic field maps, particularly those generated by Spitzer, is influenced by a variety of factors. To enhance our comprehension of the solar magnetic field, particularly its unprecedented high spatial resolution, it is essential to investigate the extent to which the accuracy of these field maps is related to the characteristics of the input images. In our study, we have developed a novel approach to evaluate the magnetic properties of individual pixels in high-resolution magnetic field maps, taking into account both the size and fraction of magnetic regions within each pixel. By employing this approach, we have been able to identify key limitations in the current assessment methods and propose new magnetic criteria, which are based on data from Retina-derived assessments. Specifically, we have demonstrated that our new criteria can accurately identify the magnetic field regions in areas of the sun where the magnetic field is fragmented. In particular, we have identified a critical threshold of 0.3 for the magnetic fill fraction, which is significantly higher than the current threshold of 0.1. Furthermore, we have shown that our new criteria can achieve an accuracy of up to 90% in correctly identifying non-polarized pixels. Additionally, we have identified specific characteristics of pixels that are misclassified, such as their tendency to have smaller magnetic regions. In particular, we have identified that misclassified pixels of one type tend to be smaller in size, while misclassified pixels of another type tend to be larger in size.

In the context of power systems, the concept of Demand Side Management (DSM) involves a continuous negotiation process among consumers and their respective central management systems. To effectively manage interactions, especially in large-scale systems, it is essential to develop strategies that can reach a stable equilibrium. Current models, which often assume a direct interaction among consumers without a central unit, have shown that individual consumers can implement a strategy to achieve a stable equilibrium. Building upon existing research, this paper first investigates how the introduction of a central unit affects the existing negotiation process. Secondly, it is shown that if consumers are aware that a central unit is managing them, they can employ a specific "trust-blind" strategy, which allows even selfish consumers to reach a stable equilibrium. Experimental results, which involve various scenarios and different system sizes, demonstrate the robustness of the proposed approach, indicating its adaptability to different practical situations.

In a (3+1)-dimensional space with anti-de Sitive boundary conditions, researchers have studied charged black strings within the framework of Rastall theory. This investigation has explored the stability of these objects against both axial and vector perturbations. Notably, incorporating quantum gravity influences has shown that the tensorial mode in axial channel exhibits enhanced stability, while the scalar-tensor mode in axial channel and all vector perturbations exhibit reduced stability. Notably, the quantum corrections have also led to significant improvements in the stability of photons traveling near the event horizon of the black string, particularly those with higher angular momentum.

When a spectral gap is absent, the convergence rates for the von Neumann Ergodic Theorem's time-averages along sequences of times t_n → ∞ are examined. This investigation extends to systems with Hausdorff dimension 1 < s < 2 that lack a conjugate point structure. The analysis reveals connections between the convergence rates and the distribution of periodic points on non-trivial horocycle orbits.

The goal of this study is to examine a potential connection between a star's iron content and the ratios of certain peaks observed in the KOI light curves, specifically the KIC 8561223 case. KIC 8561223 is a G-type star classified as either a dwarf or a giant based on its size, temperature, and surface gravity, earlier studies have found that it may have lower iron content than the average for the Milky Way's disk. The previous findings regarding its iron deficiency relied on a comparison of its spectrum with the average of the metal-poor Milky Way stars, however, this comparison was not definitive. As an alternative, it was proposed that a star's iron deficiency would be evident in the shape of its light curves, specifically the ratio between the 9000 and 10,000 angstrom ranges. To investigate this, we analyzed the light curves of 11,000 G-dwarfs in the Gaia parallax sample to see if there is a general connection between the iron content and these ratios. The analysis revealed a significant relationship between the iron content of the stars and the ratios of their peak heights, specifically the F4300/F5700 ratio, and to a lesser degree, the F5300/F4300 ratio. This connection, however, was not observed in the F5000/F4300 ratio.

This research investigates how urban growth affects fire risks in the Greater Toronto Area, by examining the correlation between fire occurrences and the number of inhabitants per block within distinct land-use areas. Temporal and spatial data on fires were analyzed separately, revealing distinct patterns in occurrence frequencies and spatial distributions across various regions. Notably, fires were observed to increase in suburban zones during summer months, whereas urban areas demonstrated a contrary trend. Moreover, our study substantiated a significant association between urbanization and fire occurrences, with suburban regions exhibiting a positive correlation, while metropolitan regions displayed a negative relationship. Ultimately, this investigation reveals that fire risk assessment necessitates a comprehensive analytical strategy encompassing temporal and spatial evaluations, thereby facilitating the development of targeted prevention measures and policy implementations aimed at mitigating urban growth-related hazards.

This study proposes a novel approach, integrating statistical processing methods with corpus techniques, to study the characteristics of natural language morphology. A unified, unified approach is developed that quantifies multiple aspects of morphology, including word form length, consistency, complexity, and structural complexity. The proposed statistical model demonstrates strong predictive capabilities in classifying languages according to their external typological features across multiple dimensions. The results indicate that simpler and more predictable languages tend to utilize nouns with complex grammatical affixes and languages with a high degree of lexicalization tend to rely on words with complex internal structures. The empirical findings obtained through this approach align with existing qualitative typological studies and the principles of morphological typology, and the proposed statistical model's performance surpasses the results of a prominent methodology in handling a dataset of 14,000 languages.

Gravitational lensing measurements of galaxy clusters are highly accurate, yet many galaxy clusters have complex substructures. The presence of substructures can lead to uncertainties in measuring the mass of the main cluster, mainly due to the concentration of baryonic matter in these substructures. To address this issue, we examined seven clusters with notable substructures and found a correlation between the amount of baryonic matter in the substructures and the uncertainty in the mass difference between the main cluster and the substructures. This correlation was discovered using two independent methods of mass measurement, indicating that the effect of substructures on the measurement is not solely due to bias but also impacts the precision of the measurements. This finding highlights the need for future studies to develop methods for separating the contribution of substructures to the overall gravitational field, such as using N-body simulations or considering the unlikelihood of certain scenarios in which substructures are present.

We investigate the computational complexity of reducing an arbitrary parameterized PDE using the kernel Hermitian Gaussian Quadrature (hGQ) method, which projects the PDE's infinite-dimensional state onto a finite-dimensional parameter space. Our analysis involves a simplified version of Burgers' equation and focuses on the performance of hGQ with two observation operators: the endpoint value and the full state. Our results indicate that hGQ significantly outperforms traditional projection methods, such as Gaussian Quadrature and Karhunen-Loève projection, especially when using the full state observation. Our analysis also reveals the importance of the observation operator choice in hGQ's performance.

Dimensionality reduction is a highly effective method for reducing the complexity of high-dimensional datasets. Several dimensionality reduction techniques, such as Isomap, MDS, and t-SNE, employ different functions to determine the reduced dimensions. Although m-Isomap offers a variation of Isomap using the m-arranged nearest neighbor approach, it shares a problem with other conditional manifold learning methods: the m value significantly impacts results, necessitating a search for an optimal m value. A novel variant of the karranged nearest neighbor approach, called m-ar-K, has been developed to overcome this limitation. By combining the karranged and arranged nearest neighbor approaches, dimensionality reduction can be achieved without being constrained by a single value. A comprehensive comparison between m-Isomap and m-ar-K methods has been conducted, highlighting that m-ar-K outperforms m-Isomap and significantly reduces computation time. Furthermore, integrating m-ar-K with a machine learning model results in an enhanced model performance.

This paper introduces a novel spatio-temporal event detection method that can identify events like train journeys or bus routes by linking distributed signal occurrences across space and time without relying on predefined parameters. The algorithm is uniquely able to adapt to changes in spatial resolution as events may span varying distances. Our results demonstrate the detection of complex patterns such as bus routes through residential, commercial, and industrial areas, and train journeys crossing bridges and tunnels. The method also offers potential applications in real-world scenarios, including urban planning, wildlife monitoring, and navigation support.

To address free boundary problems in a broader context,  $A$-harmonic functions are employed in connection with elliptic equations.  The minimal dilation of an $A$-harmonic function on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is investigated under a growth restriction. The study of minimal dilation addresses a novel type of free boundary problem that involves an $A$-epigraphical minimality condition. The research builds on previous work by Wolanski and Zhou, initially solving the problem in cases involving standard $p$-Laplace type equations.

YCo compounds, which are isomorphic in composition to Y$_{2}$Co$_{17}$, exhibit significantly higher magnetization and Curie temperatures than their counterpart Y$_{2}$Co$_{17}$. This unique characteristic, combined with Y$_{2}$Co$_{17}$$\alpha$$ isostropic behavior, could potentially make related multicompound systems like Y(Ra)$_{2}$(LiYRbNa)Co$_{17}\alpha$ promising candidates for high-temperature applications involving strong magnets. To thoroughly explore this possibility, the properties of three multicompound systems with the formula Y(Ra)$_{2}$(LiYRbNa)Co$_{17}$$\alpha$ were studied using state-of-the-art computational models and software for materials. These included VASP for computational work, USYCA and pymatgen for data analysis and structure processing, visualizing materials to ensure accuracy of input structures,从头开始 calculating the materials' magnetic properties and examining the materials' magnetostrictive and magnetostrictive coefficients ($\lambda_{\perp}$ and $\lambda_{\parallel}$), which are critical indicators of the materials' performance under magnetic fields. This allowed us to compare these properties against the benchmark material Y$_{2}$Co$_{17}$$\alpha$ and further compare them against other well-established, high-temperature magnet materials including NdFe$_

In the competitive world of construction, submitting a competitive proposal is crucial for gaining project contracts. The proposal must contain a suggested project duration and a corresponding price, with the optimal balance of bid price and risk assessment being the challenge. To address this, an innovative two-faceted bidding strategy is developed, combining data-driven bidding and an expert-driven bidding method that accurately captures loss distribution characteristics and risk propensity. The proposed bid risk tendency formulation relies on a simple, parameterizable function with well-defined properties, including positivity, continuity, and ability to represent varying risk attitudes ranging from cautious to reckless. The effectiveness of this approach is enhanced through a flexible optimization problem, which aims to maximize the potential reward by balancing profit and risk. This method is versatile, applicable to various design optimization problems, and has been successfully tested on two types of design tasks: an engineering design optimization involving a pressure vessel and a design involving a submarine pipeline, with the results demonstrating the potential for reducing design costs.

Our research investigates an in-depth analysis of the correlation between quantum negation of the Wigner function in local subsystems and non-Gaussianity of parent systems. We've established that quantum correlations are not the sole means to create Wigner negativity in a subsystem, as classical correlations can also lead to it. However, when considering symmetric subsystems within non-Gaussian, Gaussian states, it's found that classical correlations are insufficient to create Wigner negativity. Our findings highlight the crucial role that symmetry plays in determining if a subsystem's Wigner negativity is linked to quantum correlations, when considering rotations of states.

In quantum key distribution, a random number generator is essential to set an initial secure bound, $I_{sec}$. The average min-entropy, $\tilde{H}$, of the RNG directly affects this initial security threshold, prompting an investigation into the optimal $\tilde{H}$ for minimizing $I_{sec}$. This issue is particularly pertinent to de Finetti states, often generated by RNGs, and our examination reveals a counterintuitive outcome where increasing average min-entropy isn't always beneficial. This result challenges conventional assumptions, underscoring potential vulnerabilities in quantum key distribution protocols relying solely on $\tilde{H}$ for security assessments.

This research extends the concept of Bertrand curves to general metric spaces, specifically considering 3-dimensional Euclidean space with its standard metric and 3-dimensional pseudo-Euclidean space with its standard pseudo-metric.  Furthermore, the study identifies the definitive spaces for these generalized Bertrand curves and derives specific conditions for space curves to be considered as such, in terms of their Frenet curvatures.

We introduce a generalization of Subcritical/Diffusive Diffusion (SDD), a model originally proposed by Anile and Putti in 1992, to account for the evolution of populations with diverse genetic traits. This modified model, SDD-M, incorporates the analysis of two distinct scenarios based on the characteristics of the population. 

By transforming the problem, SDD-M can be re-expressed as a system of two coupled nonlinear equations, facilitating further investigation. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that these equations can be associated with specific types of optimal controls in Brascamp-Ludwig diffusion models, highlighting their mathematical relationships. 

In scenarios where the population exhibits low diversification, this problem is relevant to the study of rare disease evolution and the effects of targeted therapies. 

In contrast, when the population displays high variability, it has been connected to the effects of personalized medicine and tumor evolution, particularly in situations involving tumor suppressor genes.

In quantum feedback Qubit control, a fundamental aspect is the single qubit dynamics.
A groundbreaking method for coherently feedbacking a qubit in a one-dimensional quantum wire was developed a few years ago by Novikov et al.
This approach utilizes nanocavities to create delay lines that can store optical information.
Utilizing this delayed feedback, researchers have created single-photon quantum gates and highly entangled networks.
This thesis focuses on developing a comprehensive theoretical model, allowing for a complete and in-depth analysis of the qubit dynamics.
Our approach combines network theory methods with the self-consistent averaging technique to derive analytic equations of motion, yielding accurate results that closely match numerical calculations.
These results provide a deep understanding of how the qubit parameters can be adjusted using the delayed feedback.
Furthermore, we explore how these findings can be utilized in applications like quantum memory and quantum logic gates.

A recently proposed class of light dark matter particles known as "boosted SM dark matter" has the potential to be probed through reliable, albeit somewhat indirect, signatures in certain non-standard neutron decay channels. The notion that such neutron decays can serve as a means to study this type of dark matter has been explored in recent research. Our study delves into an examination of various natural areas in the parameter space for this specific class of dark matter by thoroughly revisiting relevant theoretical and numerical evaluations of non-standard neutron decays. Our analysis indicates the potential for laboratory experiments to reach a sensitivity nearly three orders of magnitude higher than existing constraints, primarily due to improved evaluations of the neutron's transition form factor and reduced influence from potential background factors. Furthermore, our results suggest a direct correlation between the sensitivity of various neutron decay searches and the sensitivity to the specific type of dark matter under study, thus underscoring the importance of such searches in the broader context of understanding dark matter.

This article offers an innovative approach to proving Faulhaber's Formula by utilizing Bernoulli numbers, which can also serve as a means to derive properties of both Bernoulli numbers and polynomials.

This research proposes a high-performance differential detection coding and decoding strategy for continuous phase modulation signals. By incorporating a low-rate precoder that ensures differential detection decoding can achieve the same performance as coherent detection, our approach results in a tenfold improvement in error rate over standard differential detection, closely approaching the detection and coding benchmark. Furthermore, our method resolves previously unsolvable decoding challenges by developing efficient optimization techniques, enabling even longer codeword lengths to be decoded quickly. This allows for the analysis of performance under realistic channel conditions, such as Rayleigh fading with limited power supply, where the performance gap between our approach and ideal scenarios is minimal.

Reward learning from human feedback is highly effective but resource-intensive, 
especially when models are evaluated individually. Batch comparisons, however, 
allow multiple models to be evaluated simultaneously, increasing efficiency. In 
this research, we introduce techniques to generate the optimal human feedback 
queries, taking into account both the underlying reward structure and the limits of 
human attention. Our approach leads to a robust, black-box optimization algorithm 
that adjusts the optimization strategy based on human limitations. When tested on 
a variety of real-world optimization problems, our method significantly outperformed 
human estimates, increasing performance by up to 22% for certain tasks.

Recent findings indicate a discrepancy between theoretical and experimental data for nucleon structure functions in certain ranges of x-Bjorken, which may be attributed to the effects of noncommutativity and nonassociativity of space. Surprisingly, incorporating corrections related to noncommutativity yields a satisfactory alignment of theoretical and experimental data even without adjusting other structure function parameters. Furthermore, the observed discrepancy seems to be absent in another relevant range of x-Bjorken, which serves as a strong indicator that space noncommutativity does not significantly impact structure functions.

Quantum systems isolated from their environment settle into their lowest energy configurations, known as ground states. In the context of spin systems on a square lattice, we explore how frustration and nonlinearity affect the two-body entanglement patterns in the ground states. Our analysis reveals that two types of two-body entanglement, the Wilson and entanglement spectrum entanglement, respond significantly to the complex interplay of frustration and nonlinearity. Notably, our findings indicate that both types of entanglement exhibit characteristics of topological order, which can be influenced by frustration and nonlinearity. This is particularly evident from the two-fold degeneracy of the ground states, the two-component nature of the entanglement spectrum, and the emergence of anyonic anyon anyon anyon phases due to frustration and nonlinearity. Consequently, the entanglement properties of the ground states serve as a reliable indicator of frustration and nonlinearity driven topological order.

For random Hermitian matrices with Gaussian-distributed, complex off-diagonal and real diagonal entries, we investigate the impact of the off-diagonal band width, denoted by W, on the eigenvalue distribution. As W increases, we find that the distribution of complex eigenvalues converges to a semicircular profile, while for smaller values of W, we demonstrate that this circular law does not hold. Additionally, we derive an explicit formula for the joint density of complex eigenvalues, revealing connections to previous studies on the GUE, GUE-BOE, and specific random graph models.

Although pre-trained language models have made significant advancements in dialogue analysis, they primarily rely on sequential input-output examples, failing to capture the complex semantic connections underlying dialogue interactions. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel task called semantic connection graph learning for dialogue, which requires learning the relationships between dialogue segments. Our study demonstrates that these connections can be effectively represented using graph neural networks, which can be trained end-to-end with the help of pre-trained language models. A key advantage of this new task formulation is that it enables the exploration of both weakly and fully supervised settings, thus making it more versatile and widely applicable. We show that existing language models can be successfully adapted to solve this new task in a weakly supervised framework, yielding results comparable to those of strong baselines trained with full annotations.

As interpretability models rise in importance for trust and ethics, it's crucial to grasp their inner workings. Although this need has been recognized, there's a gap in understanding how to measure an algorithm's interpretability. This work aims to fill that gap by developing an innovative approach to measure the interpretability of algorithms that use language, based on their ability to be understood. After defining and testing this measure, we found that it can be used to compare different types of algorithms and identify ways to make them more transparent. The results show that incorporating more context in this comparison is important and that our approach can be applied across different types of data and problems. This research provides an essential foundation for improving algorithmic interpretability, especially in areas where issues of trust and fairness are paramount.

Anomaly detection using the Isolation Forest method is crucial in analyzing financial transactions, as it helps identify unusual patterns in a dataset. The algorithm functions by randomly selecting hyperplanes to segment the data and calculating the depth of data points based on these divisions, marking points with higher depths as potential anomalies. This study aims to refine the Isolation Forest by integrating concepts from fuzzy sets, using a fuzzy approach to identify anomalies. With this method, anomalies can be detected across datasets of uniform dimensionality, and the integration of fuzzy principles enhances the algorithm's accuracy. Our approach involved modifying the Isolation Forest with adjustments that account for the likelihood of a data point being anomalous, using the integration of isolation and forest scores. Empirical results on real-world data confirm that the refined Isolation Forest yields better outcomes compared to the standard Isolation Forest.

In a hierarchical Bayesian model designed to analyze paired data with extreme outliers, each data pair is evaluated for outlier status using a binary variable. Binary outcomes are governed by a logistic function influenced by a shared parameter m, which also determines how many data pairs are excluded. This study focuses on estimating m, noting that incorrect estimates can lead to biased parameter estimates and reduced estimation accuracy. A proposed two-step method first calculates m's posterior distribution, then re-evaluates it in light of model residuals, adjusting for dependence. Results from a Monte Carlo experiment confirm the method's reliability, demonstrating minimal sensitivity to m's initial estimates and improved convergence rates when utilizing the second step.

In positions with multiple values, a unique differential equation has been discovered, which describes the evolution of a particular type of symmetric shapes. This discovery was first reported by multiple authors including Bertozzi, Chang, Chodankiewicz, Garavoglia, Huang, and Vial. By integrating the results from the equation, it was possible to determine the properties of a distinct and significant set of symmetric shapes for both two- and three-dimensional spheres. The characteristics of the general group of symmetric shapes can be understood through the results from this distinct set.

More than two decades ago, SmiRnOVa's "Alice in Wonderland" showcased the potential for virtual literary creation using symbolic knowledge models. Since then, progress in neural models, enhanced by extensive training datasets, has significantly improved the capabilities of storytelling. Notably, the 2020 ATOMIC challenge has demonstrated remarkable advancements, surpassing previous leading commonsense knowledge knowledge bases in F1 score by 16%. Despite these achievements, prior studies have primarily relied on external knowledge sources, while the integration of novel semantic patterns via systematic perturbation of stories and specific character actions remains largely unexplored. In order to evaluate the effectiveness of systematic semantic perturbation, we have expanded the ATOMIC dataset by 20%, resulting in a new resource known as ATOMIC20. Our study reveals the positive impact of this novel knowledge base on semantic perturbation, with our systematic approach yielding a 200% increase in the resource size. Furthermore, our study highlights the importance of incorporating diverse semantic patterns when training knowledge models, as exemplified by the performance of a neural model, fine-tuned on ATOMIC20, outperforming its predecessor, ShPOM, in multiple tasks. These findings not only advance our understanding of knowledge-based storytelling, but also demonstrate the significant role that systematic semantic perturbation can play in this field.

This article outlines the data processing steps taken by the Hi-GAL survey which utilizes IRASACA data from the Herschel Space Observatory. We describe the modifications made to the standard IRASACA data to improve quality and then detail the simulation conducted to evaluate the survey's performance and estimate its ability to detect faint sources. We also describe the implementation of source detection and beam smoothing applied to the survey data.

The elemental abundances of stars in the Milky Way's globular clusters show significant variation. To understand the origins of these differences, a model simulating the dynamic evolution of four specific clusters has been developed. The simulation combines key processes including supernova-induced star ejections, internal migration, and star-induced gas expansion, all within a moving framework that accurately represents the external galaxy's influence. The simulated external forces include orbital decay, tidal disruption, and gradual loss of members due to the age of each cluster. The outcomes of the simulation show promising results in replicating the elemental composition variations of four specific GCs, particularly the effects of supernova-induced star ejections and gas expansion. Furthermore, it has been discovered that early gas expansion can enhance these effects, demonstrating that these processes have important implications for the evolution of molecular clouds and star formation.

In one-dimensional systems, a fundamental issue arises when balancing speed and accuracy: any increase in velocity inevitably leads to a significant drop in precision. This velocity-accuracy relationship has been observed in numerical simulations and theoretical models. This phenomenon is particularly pronounced in real-world scenarios involving particles with random motion, which has been overlooked in existing mathematical models that rely heavily on numerical solutions. This study presents an innovative mathematical approach to tackle this trade-off, which is based on particles exhibiting random motion. By adapting traditional mathematical methods to account for this dynamic, we are able to achieve a mathematical solution that is viable in a variety of one-dimensional systems, which can be verified through numerical simulations. This study demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to three distinct physical systems, which have been previously investigated experimentally and theoretically.

Recent discussions surrounding the Many Worlds Interpretation of quantum mechanics often cite the Frauchiger-Renner thought experiment as strong evidence. However, Frauchiger-Renner's scenario isn't unique in highlighting potential issues, as it shares key features with no-collapse theories and quantum mechanics that violate no-signalling. A comparable situation arises in an analogous version of no-collapse theories involving Hardy's setup, which can be considered as "hardy's no-collapse" in contrast to "renner's no-collapse". Utilizing quantum control theory, we demonstrate that the seemingly contradictory outcomes in Hardy's no-collapse and renner's no-collapse can be resolved without NO-CLASSICAL assumptions typically required by the no-collapse argument. Furthermore, these analogous situations reveal that the measurement problem isn't unique to the many-worlds interpretation, as both the theory and time-like entanglement exhibit certain puzzling characteristics.

The behavior of massless free quantum field theories under scalar transformations reveals distinct responses to periodic and Dirichlet boundary conditions, indicating a fundamental difference between them. This variances suggests that conditions as straightforward as the Dirichlet do not universally apply across all contexts, while the significant differences observed may have minimal impact on typical quantum field theory calculations, such as those involving Casimir effects and Schramm loop statistics. The underlying source of this asymmetry is the different mathematical properties of determinants associated with the Laplacians under periodic and Dirichlet conditions, specifically their connections to Riemann surfaces.

Using computer assistance, we have found that the fifth algebraic transfer d$5\to 20$ over $\mathbb{F}_2$ is injective on certain generated elements, including those not previously proven to be non-zero in this transfer. The proof of its injectivity relied on a novel criterion developed by the authors, which distinguing generators from their colleagues in the algebra's generating set.

This study examines how a molecular hydrogen (H2) absorption filter blocks Lyman-alpha photons based on pressure, and demonstrates the feasibility of adjusting the pressure in the filter to prevent the leakage of these photons to the geosynchronous satellite, CNES-GALILEO. The experiment measured the transmittance of the filter at different pressures between 0.01 and 0.1 Torr using the SHF radiometer on board the satellite, with a result of a 30-40% reduction in transmitted photons within the bandpass of the filter, relative to its peak, over a 0.08 Torr pressure range.

This research introduces a decentralized strategy for optimizing the balance between performance and communication expenses. The approach involves multiple agents working together, exchanging only essential information. By doing so, the team can achieve similar results to the centralized system within reasonable communication costs. To achieve this optimization, the decentralized strategy incorporates a cost-effective communication algorithm and applies it to each agent, thus maintaining overall system performance at a minimal communication expense. To validate the effectiveness of this approach, a real-world case study is conducted using the well-known Tank benchmark, with the results demonstrating the tradeoff between communication costs and performance metrics, specifically a measure of the agents' proximity to the optimal solution over time.

Robust copy detection is achieved by combining active indexing, which ranks images to efficiently utilize a limited budget, and advanced neural networks that capture detailed visual similarities, thereby mitigating the errors caused by active indexing. However, the current synergy relies on manually determined, hard active indexing scores, which can lead to a loss of accuracy due to false positives in the initial retrieval. To overcome this limitation, we introduce Soft Score, a novel approach that integrates active indexing and deep visual similarity in a weighted manner, with the optimal weights determined by the task at hand. By employing the Soft Score framework, we demonstrate its superior performance in copy detection, surpassing the hard active indexing baseline and even outperforming GridNet, a leading copy detection method, on a variety of datasets.

This paper explores a modified authentication method, in which an authenticator receives a long and complex message from an incoming claimant. The message is generated using a code with a specific error-correcting method. By choosing codes that produce an arbitrarily small probability of error, the researchers demonstrate that a secure system can operate under a specific constraint: as the message length increases, the amount of information per symbol approaches zero. Moreover, the claimed information must adhere to the code's parity-check constraints, and the researchers analyze scenarios involving both truthful and deceptive claims. What's more, the message can be transmitted over a noisy channel, and the researchers derive conditions for secure communication even in the presence of adversarial interference. Interestingly, the conditions required for deceptive claims and those that are not deceptive are complementary. As a result, the system's security improves when the channel has higher noise levels. Furthermore, the researchers examine additional authentication systems based on a specific variant of polar codes that achieve a specific constraint, and they derive a formula for optimal system performance.

A long-standing controversy surrounds the phase diagrams of particles in weakly disordered systems.  A key proposed feature, the Griffiths phase, is characterized by the system's long-range correlations.  To investigate the binned velocity autocorrelation function in this context, we've examined the dynamics of a 1D chain of Brownian particles within a tilted periodic landscape.  Using binned coarse-graining techniques and varying system sizes, we've applied a test to determine the existence of superdiffusion and identified a superdiffusion exponent of about 0.8.  This study reveals a superdiffusion exponent that matches the theoretical prediction and confirms the presence of a Griffiths phase in this system.

A new method has been developed to assess the economic impact of financial disruptions by utilizing high-frequency data on stock prices. This technique focuses on the changes in the cross-sectional volatility of industry stock prices as an indicator of the effects of financial shocks on the financial sector's industry composition. Empirical evidence shows that small stock price price fluctuations have a temporary and positive effect on industries' cash flow sensitivity to credit, whereas large declines in stock prices have a long-lasting negative effect on corporate investment and credit availability. Our approach allows us to quantify the cumulative impact of sequential financial disruptions on the economy and to examine the effects of the 2008 financial crisis on the economy's performance in the subsequent years.

Kinetic angular momentum is consistently generated due to the friction caused by galaxy movement in the dark matter environment. This friction causes recoil in dark matter particles that can be expressed as a function of recoil energy produced by galaxy movement and the particle mass. The recoil problem has been solved for particles in the free-fall regime and in galactic collapse into dense halos through the use of an inhomogeneous Einstein-Boltzmann equation. This new approach to recoil has been incorporated into existing numerical codes that simulate galaxy collapse, such as CAMB and CMBLenin, by representing the dark matter particles as a continuum. The implementation of this approach has been done for three types of particle masses in the eV range. The results show that the dark matter recoil significantly affects galaxy rotation curves, galaxy clustering, and the primordial fluctuations. This effect is particularly noticeable for light fermions and bosons, which have a significant recoil that opposes the movement of galaxies and recoil momentum that opposes kinetic angular momentum in the dark matter halos. This effect leads to a slight particle drift and a small recoil that doesn't significantly impact kinetic angular momentum in dark matter halos. The dark matter recoil may explain some anomalies in galaxy rotation curves and the need for a new parameterization in this field.

Our proposed FGNET-RH approach enhances entity classification accuracy by
refining word and context representations using a relation encoder. This object-
oriented representation scheme leverages prior knowledge to optimize typing
efficiency. A novel attention framework is also presented that effectively
connects the relation encoder and the network, thus improving overall model
performance. Additionally, a new entity linking model based on graph neural
networks is developed to accurately identify mention entities within a specific
language context. Evaluation on the Microscale Knowledge Graph Completion
benchmark demonstrates that FGNET-RH achieves notable performance improvements
in entity typing. Moreover, ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of the
representation and attention frameworks, and the application of knowledge graph
embeddings in entity typing.

A specific form of a univalent function, $f(z)$, is defined by the expression
$$
\frac{zf'(z)}{f(z)}-1=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}a_{j+1}(j+1)z^{\frac{2}{\beta}j},
$$
where $\beta$ is a real number greater than or equal to one. The research focuses on determining functions $M$ and $m$ for the Stieltus transform $s(f)(t)$ under specified conditions involving $t$ and $\eta$ where $t$ varies over the unit disk and $-1 \leq \eta < 1$. The research investigates subordination relations between $s(f)(t)$ and $t$ as well as suggests conjectures regarding the bounds of $s(f)(t)$ for $M$ and $m$. These findings are further supported by related hypotheses concerning $\beta$-univalent functions. The research also presents consequences derived from the established Stieltus transform relations.

In virtualized cloud computing, preprocessing scheduling methods aim to optimize resource usage by distributing tasks across machines. However, these methods face a challenge: they rely on predicting future VM behavior, which proves difficult due to the unpredictable and rapidly changing patterns of applications. To address this issue, we introduce Prepartition, a novel task scheduling approach that sidesteps the forecasting problem. By shifting from application-level resource forecasting to machine-level prepartitioning, Prepartition anticipates changes in virtual machines ahead of time, minimizing service disruptions. This method evaluates machine parts independently, determines their resource requirements, and scales them accordingly. As a result, Prepartition scales linearly with the size of a cluster, ensuring efficient resource management. Simulation results demonstrate that Prepartition reduces the likelihood of unexpected service scaling by as much as 20%, compared to other scheduling methods. This improvement translates into better overall resource allocation, especially under dynamic workloads.

In the realm of game theory and artificial intelligence, solving complex, high-dimensional games is a crucial yet computationally demanding task. To address this challenge, our research introduces a novel approach, Nash-FPN, a neural network architecture capable of accurately predicting equilibria in high-dimensional games. We found that our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods by a significant margin, with improvements of over 30%. Furthermore, our study reveals that our approach fosters more efficient multi-agent learning by achieving high prediction accuracy with lower average regret than other methods after a relatively short time. The effectiveness of our approach is supported by our experiments on two crucial real-world tasks: social learning and multi-agent reinforcement learning.

This study introduces a novel approach to bringing innovative findings to life in laboratory settings. Building on recent advances in empirical causal analysis, we show how cutting-edge reduction-dimensional techniques and massive-scale simulations can enhance bias-variance trade-offs. Empirical evidence suggests that combining these methods can substantially improve experimental power without significantly increasing bias. As a result, innovative methods can be tested more efficiently and effectively in laboratories, leading to faster advancements in causal models. Diminishing returns in improving causal models may cause us to overlook the benefits of novel approaches due to entrenched methodologies. Our proposed framework enables efficient and effective testing of causal models, allowing for rapid advancements and reducing reliance on established methods.

This research focuses on real-time detection of covert attacks in dynamic systems. The method developed here relies on statistical data from system measurements, incorporating uncertainty to identify unusual patterns. By separating the uncertainty into two components - one related to system dynamics and the other to measurement errors - difficult to interpret system behaviors can be simplified into a more manageable form. Measurement errors are represented as probability distributions over a grid. Although calculating these probabilities can be computationally expensive for fine grids, approximating them using coarse grids reduces the complexity. Consequently, system monitoring can be efficiently carried out across a range of values. To validate this method, it was applied to a power plant boiler, a common industrial benchmark, and successful detection of a hidden fault was achieved without significantly increasing computational costs, even with 100 grid points.

To create concise summaries of lengthy, structured academic papers titled and outlined with subheadings, we introduce GAE-ISumm, an enhanced graph attention encoder-decoder model. Building upon the existing IArSum model, we incorporate an additional attention mechanism that focuses on the connections within conceptual ideas to generate accurate summaries. IArSum initially captures the context using an encoder, an attention network, and connectivity between semantically related concepts, which are then combined in a decoder to produce the summary. In this study, we refine IArSum by incorporating three main advancements. First, we replace its word-level components with word vector-based components, leading to better capture of contextual relationships and increased robustness. Second, we replace its sentence-level attention mechanism with one rooted in active learning theory, which further improves contextual representation. Finally, we replace its semantic connectivity mechanism with one based on word vectors and sentence embeddings, enabling more effective connectivity between concepts. We test our model using the IArSum dataset and compare its performance with various baselines, resulting in improved summary quality and higher coherence and coherence scores.

Given an additive subcategory $\mathcal{S}$ of Mod(A) consisting of A's modules, and defining $\textbf{Mod}(\mathcal{S})$ as the full subcategory of exact sequences in Mod(A) consisting of modules from $\mathcal{S}$, we establish conditions under which $\textbf{Mod}(\mathcal{S})$ is itself a bireflexive Grothendieck category. Furthermore, when certain criteria are satisfied, the scalar category $\mathcal{A}/\mathcal{S}$ emerges as a Grothendieck category. Additionally, when certain conditions are met, independent S-rings (A) of Krull type (A) arise, where each module in such an S-ring (A) possesses nontrivial presentations within Mod(S).
