The popular t-SVD approach has been a subject of research for improvement. The existing algorithms for S-TRAN require multiple passes through the data to process each rank-k factor matrix, making them less efficient. In response, we have developed a novel, efficient randomized algorithm for t-SVD that needs only one pass over the data tensor to compute each rank-k factor matrix. The algorithm leverages an outer product structure in the data to reduce computation time, while also enabling parallel processing. Our analysis shows that the new algorithm is both theoretically sound and practical, demonstrating at least a 100x speedup over existing methods in real-world applications.

Recent advancements in graph neural networks have generated significant interest in leveraging machine learning techniques for graph data processing.  Graph embedding, a key graph neural network component, translates graph data into a low-dimensional vector space.  However, existing graph embedding techniques mainly focus on static graph data, whereas real-world graph data is inherently dynamic and evolves over time.  This paper proposes Temporal Embedding, a novel framework designed to map dynamic graph data into a low-dimensional time-stamped vector format.  Temporal Embedding builds upon the success of node2vec, a popular algorithm for static graph data processing, and adapts it to handle dynamic graph data through three main modifications.  These modifications include (1) the integration of real-time graph data into the algorithm, (2) the incorporation of predictions for missing graph data, and (3 the extension of neighbor relationships to encompass time-based relationships.  A significant challenge in temporal graph data processing lies in accurately predicting the time-based relationships between graph nodes.  This paper's Temporal Embedding approach addresses this issue by using predictive modeling to generate time-based relationship probabilities.  A key advantage of Tempional Embedding is its ability to accurately predict both existing and potentially new graph data relationships with high precision.  This paper's experimental results demonstrate that Temporal Embedding significantly outperforms existing methods in node classification and link prediction tasks on various benchmark datasets.

Our research focused on examining whether the narrow low-energy resonance attributed to the isobaric analog state of $^7$He within the $^6$He-$^7$He system actually exists. Utilizing the Rosenbluth technique to measure the cross-sectional differential, we analyzed the $^3$He($^7$He, $e^+$ $e^-$) $^3$He reaction at 450 MeV. This was the first time the cross-sectional data for the excitation of a 7He isobaric analog state at 2.52 MeV was directly observed, with the measured width of the resonance being 0.84 MeV. Our results indicate that the cross-sectional data's real part is consistent with the theoretical predictions derived from the mirror nucleus $^7$Li. This finding is supported by the theoretical density distribution. Furthermore, the observed discrepancy between the measured and theoretical imaginary potential values suggests that the 2s-$1\delta$ mixing in the $^7$He resonance width may be a contributing factor.

The study of Nirenberg problems on half spheres from a geometric perspective is explored this year.  On full spheres, solutions to the prescribed scalar curvature problem typically exhibit a limited number of blow-up points and asymptotically resemble a sum of bubbles.  However, solutions to the Nirenberg problem on half spheres can demonstrate an infinite number of blow-up points, and localised blow-up occurs under specific conditions.  In contrast to solutions on full spheres, Nirenberg problems on n-dimensional half spheres exhibit non-uniqueness for n ≥ 4.  Furthermore, for dimensions n = 2, 3, and prescribed boundary conditions, we discover the existence of non-trivial solutions through a combination of Lusternik-Schnirelmann category theory and symmetry considerations.

A challenge in learning discriminative embedding spaces is that traditional methods that use instance-wise similarity often produce non-uniform distributions, making it difficult for models to learn a consistent representation. Addressing this issue, a new approach called Deep Class-wise Discrepancy Loss (DCDL) was proposed. By applying a novel loss function called Discrepancy Loss (DL) to evaluate the similarity of data points within the same class, DCDRL aims to produce a more uniform distribution and thus, improve the discriminative power of the embedding space. By comparing the DC components of the Volterra series representation of class-wise features, DCDRL effectively measures the similarity between data points and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, as demonstrated in studies involving large-scale face recognition and few-shot learning tasks.

As the United Kingdom's initial COVID-19 case was identified in January 2020, researchers began exploring strategies to curb the pandemic's spread, with particular emphasis on contact tracing. Researchers from Oxford and Cambridge universities initiated a study to assess the impact of UK's Test and Trace service in mitigating COVID-19 spread, alongside a parallel project to enhance its effectiveness. One of the enhancements, partnerships with local authorities, involved setting up offices in high-risk areas, boosting the number of testers, and promoting testing. To evaluate the influence of these partnerships on Test and Trace's overall performance, researchers conducted a comprehensive evaluation in areas with and without local involvement, as well as a nationwide analysis. Surprisingly, local partnerships yielded only modest benefits, with minimal impact on testing rates or compliance. However, when considering COVID-19 cases averted, researchers discovered that approximately 1,000 cases were prevented per week due to Test and Trace, a figure that significantly increased to around 1,500 in areas featuring local partnerships. These partnerships led to higher testing rates, increased testing duration, improved testing and compliance rates, more frequent close contact reporting, increased vaccination uptake, enhanced compliance with isolation and social distancing, improved vaccination prioritization, and heightened awareness of COVID-19 and its treatment options. Using a combination of a generalized mass-light profile and a Radial Velocity dataset, the gravitational mass and metallicity of the star cluster Melotte 72 are estimated. Through a process called dynamical relaxation, it's estimated that the cluster's current state is far from equilibrium, and its estimated mass is found to be relatively small. Furthermore, the cluster's age, estimated to be around 2 billion years, indicates that it's among the younger clusters, and thus, it has a relatively long lifespan, and through metallicity analysis, it's estimated that the cluster has a relatively high metal content, and through a process called accretion, it's estimated that the cluster has a relatively low metal content.

We investigate the levels of excursions from random fields on an $L$-sided polygon that satisfy the condition $\sigma^2=1/L-1$ and a zero boundary constraint. As $L$ approaches infinity, we find that the transition from one phase to another occurs abruptly, resulting in a significant change in the excursions' behavior, which can be described as "excursion condensation." Our analysis reveals that this phase transition corresponds to the percolation threshold for long-range percolation, a concept originally proposed by Aizenman and Baccardi. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive description of the excursions' behavior above and below this threshold, taking into consideration fields of varying symmetry classes, including Gaussian, GUE, and super Schramm-Loewner Evolution.

Directly applying regression often outperforms traditional approaches in camera calibration tasks, however it has a major drawback: the results are illogical as it disregards the underlying properties of geometric transformations. Our investigation builds on previous findings that a regression-based method can be formulated as an optimization problem with a linear objective function and a structured uncertainty term. Additionally, our work demonstrates that a different type of constraint - a hard constraint - is particularly effective in maintaining reasonability in camera calibration tasks. Additionally, our experiments show that this constraint surpasses traditional reasoning-based methods in maintaining reasonability while incorporating more information and yielding better performance in camera calibration.

Learning human-like skills from interactive observation has long been a primary
goal in artificial intelligence. The most effective method, inverse reinforcement
learning, can be enhanced by using learned human motion as a set of guiding
constraints. This approach allows expert knowledge to be applied in a versatile
manner, enabling the use of unverified motion data as implicit expert preferences.
However, using these implicit preferences in reinforcement learning can be
problematic, as it may lead to overfitting, especially when using discrete time
discretization. In contrast, using high-dimensional continuous constraints
associated with specific time points results in overfitting, as the agent may
prioritize these constraints over other aspects of the environment. To address
this issue, we propose explicitly enabling the agent to query learned human
motion at relevant time points, thus avoiding overfitting. This approach is
demonstrated on challenging robotic manipulation tasks with impressive results.

Establishing a spatial map of the Milky Way is a core goal of the Gaia mission, which is essential for understanding the structure of the galaxy and how galaxy formation processes interact with its substructures. Thanks to Gaia's unique capabilities, our knowledge of the galaxy is rapidly expanding, allowing us to identify the shapes of its various substructures and understand their interconnectedness. This paper presents an analysis of SDSS-APM3.5J, a vast and distinct galaxy discovered in 2017, utilizing data from the DR2 mission to examine its position, motion, and three-dimensional structure. Utilizing the full-sample Gaia DR2 parallax and proper motion data, we identified 1,279 member stars associated with this galaxy and, through a Bayesian analysis, derived its galactic plane coordinates, distance, and kinematic properties. Furthermore, we were able to confirm the galaxy's three-dimensional shape and observed its orientation relative to the galactic plane. This study showcases Gaia's ability to uncover new galactic substructures, which serves as a crucial step towards grasping the underlying mechanisms of the galaxy's formation.

In our research, we leverage the tree structure of the treewidth problem to develop efficient algorithms for classical graph problems like Vertex Cover and MaxCut. By combining this approach with the balanced separation of the graph, we formulate an optimization problem for tree decomposition that results in linear time complexity for algorithms using a balanced separation based tree decomposition. We further illustrate that this method can be applied to a range of problems, leading to improved results and efficient fixed-parameter algorithms for problems with polynomial kernel.

The analysis of network clustering is crucial in understanding local characteristics of complex networks, yet creating a suitable continuous clustering coefficient for weighted networks remains challenging. A commonly used clustering method in weighted networks is the Zhang--Horvath (H Zhang) coefficient, but its continuous nature is questionable. This study evaluates H Zhang's clustering in networks of varying sizes and dimensions, as well as in empirical networks, to understand its behavior and suitability. The analysis reveals similarities in clustering behavior between H Zhang's coefficient and a new proposed coefficient, but H Zhang's interpretation of clustering strength differs from the traditional clustering coefficient and local correlation measures. The new coefficient is suggested as a more natural approach to studying weighted network clustering, with the study also highlighting the difficulties in analyzing weighted networks and the need for further research in this area.

The accuracy of predictions made by physics-informed neural networks can be certified using rigorous error estimates developed after the fact. These error estimates, previously established for elliptic problems and now extended to advection-diffusion problems, are adapted for use with neural network solutions. The new estimates leverage both the neural network solution and traditional finite element methods. Our experiments highlight the practical value of these error estimates in guiding the optimization of EINN models and providing accuracy guarantees for neural network solutions.

Covariance models play a fundamental role in creating air pollution models. This study introduces a new approximation of the Interpolate and Map Kriging model, a conventional spatial air pollution model. By first approximating the spatial process through an advanced kriging approach and then using this approximation in the model, the method handles large number of monitoring stations efficiently. A generalized linear model is approximated by replacing the spatial component with its kriged version and applying linearization. This kriged generalized linear model is then transformed into a suitable least squares problem with additional 'inducing variables', the inducing variables' locations of which are optimized using a self-adaptive approach. A suitable indicator function is used to evaluate model performance and test validation shows the method's effectiveness, with successful applications of the novel model predicting concentrations for fine particulate matter across Europe.

In numerical studies of the 300-site triangular-lattice p-wave superconductor that includes both time-reversal symmetry-respecting physical pairs and unphysical single-wedge pairs, researchers found that even after eliminating the majorana-induced zero-energy peak, a significant contribution remains. This contribution rapidly diminishes with increasing temperature due to a high density of non-majorana zero-energy states. A simulation with time-dependent quasi-adiabatic deformation showed that the unphysical states are accessible via continuous deformation but not through non-adaptive manipulation. This research highlights that the raw fidelity of the ground state may not be reliable for experimentally verifying topological properties, suggesting the necessity of developing new methods for confirming topological states.

This paper introduces new bounds for the spectral properties of the Gram matrix in linear bandits, which could potentially lead to improved limits on the regret for model selection and hard parameter aggregation, especially for problems involving non-generic designs. We demonstrate how this knowledge can be applied and provide practical methods for designing exploration strategies in an exploration exploitation algorithm. Our experimental results show that utilizing these spectral bounds leads to enhanced performance on model selection, clustering, and finding the optimal arm. Our findings also contribute to regression analysis by offering empirical and practical insights that were previously absent.

The orbital hall effect, which is a unique property of light atoms, can be used to study local phase changes, offering insight into a clearer signature of this phenomenon compared to the valley hall effect. Our approach involves using the orbital current as a tool to investigate the valence bond structure, specifically in a model of a dimer chain, which is based on a local representation of two orbital bases. This method is similar to measuring bond charges, but it is more sensitive to complex orbital interactions and local phase changes, resulting in the ability to identify detailed patterns of positive and negative orbital currents that correspond to specific physical phenomena, such as dimers, long-range interactions, and odd-dimensional fermions.

The rise of adversarial machine learning has cast doubt on the reliability of artificial intelligence systems, prompting a need for more robust solutions. While previous research focused on evaluating model resilience through evaluation techniques, the solutions proposed to date have been relatively scarce. We have already established methods for developing robust classifiers using reinforcement learning, but these come at a significant computational cost. To alleviate this concern, this study investigates whether the effectiveness of reinforcement-learned robust classifiers can be enhanced through post-training methods. We demonstrate the effectiveness of applying additional post-training techniques to existing robust classifiers, significantly improving their adversarial resilience while reducing computational overhead. Moreover, our approach allows for the creation of compact, yet powerful, models capable of withstanding sophisticated attacks. We further validate the utility of our techniques in real-world scenarios by examining their impact on image forgery detection through gradient reversal modules and knowledge distillation methods.

A particular challenge in combining multi-mission catalogs is accurately pairing individual entries, especially when dealing with complex celestial sources such as AGNs and star-forming galaxies, which consist of multiple distinct point-like structures. To overcome this limitation, our study utilized a vast dataset comprising 1.6 billion photometric measurements from NASA's WISE and JWISE missions and analyzed approximately 270,000 locations containing both single and multiple structures. We successfully refined the techniques for matching these sources, leveraging an additional 0.01-0.1 magnitude of photometric information and leveraging the full spatial extent of each object to extend the range of possible matches. The incorporation of machine learning was found to be an effective approach in extending the range of possible matches. As a result, our methods can be applied to a wider variety of source distributions, and our study provides a detailed characterization of the possibilities and limitations of matching sources, including a comprehensive analysis of cross-match probabilities as a function of source separation and photometric differences. Our methods have already been applied to a sample of 1.6 million galaxies and have revealed previously undetected structures, demonstrating the potential of our techniques to significantly enhance astronomical research.

The concept of 'nowhere stationary' for a subset of cardinals can be understood in the context of the first $\kappa$ elements of $\kappa^+$. A set $A$ within $\kappa^+$ is considered 'nowhere stationary' if no tail of $A$ interacts with a stationary collection. This notion arises from the research of Galvin and Kaminski. A notable outcome shows that any maximal 'nowhere stationary' set among sets of size $\kappa^+$ has the property of being non-Ramsey. Furthermore, this finding can be generalized. A broader definition considers $\mathcal{F}$ to be 'nowhere $\kappa^+$-reflecting' if, for every $\alpha$ beyond $\kappa$, there exists a subset $B$ within $\alpha$ of size $\kappa$ which is disjoint from $\{\beta \in \operatorname{Lim}(\kappa) \mid \beta \text{ is } \kappa\text{-reflecting}\}$. This concept expands on the 'nowhere stationary' idea. This broader definition can be utilized to create more intricate counterexamples, such as a $\kappa^+$-sized collection exhibiting the $\square_\kappa$ property that is considered 'nowhere $\kappa^+$-reflecting'.

OntoPlot is an innovative visualization platform for ontologies that operates through a class diagram layout, allowing for the seamless integration of diverse diagram types. It can process and display ontologies from various sources, such as OWL and RDF/Turtle formats, and can be either typed or untyped. Key features include class grouping, property edge styling, multilingual class labeling, class attribute display, class instance representation, and the import of external data from various sources. Additionally, OntoPlot offers an interactive interface for zooming, panning, searching, and filtering, as well as exporting options in various formats, including PDF, SVG, image files, and code in languages such as Python and JavaScript. It also supports real-time data streaming for interactive realisation. This tool is accessible as a web application for free, along with a commercial version offering extra features like company branding, single-sign-on, customisation, training, API access, and automated hosting and sharing.

We introduce an innovative approach utilizing CycleGAN for the cross-domain retrieval of 3D point clouds, incorporating data augmentation techniques to maintain original input characteristics and increase generic applicability. Initially, we employ CycleGAN to create a general transformation network capable of adapting to various datasets without extensive retraining. Next, we leverage this model to produce a cyclic loss function augmented with additional terms preserving input structural integrity and point distribution, thereby maintaining input characteristics during domain translation. Experimental results indicate superior performance over state-of-the-art methods across multiple benchmark datasets and demonstrate the augmented approach's success with new, unseen datasets.

Thanks to advances in deep learning, generative models have significantly improved at producing realistic samples from real-world sensory data. However, generating a vast amount of data requires significant computational power, making it necessary to utilize large-scale computing resources, which in turn makes interactions with scientific devices or experiments impractical due to limitations in physical computing power. As a result, we propose using generative models to develop more efficient, intelligent systems capable of managing and optimizing interactions between software and hardware due to learned patterns in data generation.

A theoretical framework is developed to predict the thermal diffusion factor for mixtures of uncharged molecules under temperature gradients. This theoretical framework is notable for its consideration of the flexibility and the effects of temperature and pressure on the thermal diffusion factor. Specifically, the thermal diffusion factor is expressed in terms of the rotational polarizability and translational-rotational energy exchange, which are in turn expressed in terms of the molecular dipole moment and polarizability. This theoretical framework is applied to the prediction of the thermal diffusion factor in short polyethylene and polypropylene chains, and the results are compared with experimental data. Furthermore, the application of the framework to pretreated polyethylene and polypropylene chains reveals the potential for manipulating the thermal diffusion factor through surface treatments such as corona discharge, electroless metal deposition, and anodization.

Recent research has showcased transformer-based models' success in automatically grading essays. These large models have shown impressive accuracy, reaching up to a maximum F1 score of 0.810, but their computational cost is substantial, with each model parameter costing thousands of dollars to obtain and billions of parameters requiring tens to hundreds of gigabytes of memory for inference.  To overcome this limitation, we investigate a more efficient, high-performance, low-cost alternative by using a number of smaller fine-tuned models with around 100 million parameters to achieve comparable results to larger, pre-trained transformers.  By using a number of different settings, including different initial numbers of parameters and different training strategies, we successfully fine-tuned our models to achieve scores as high as 0.809, just a small 1% behind the top-scoring transformer-based model.  Our top-scoring model, after being trained with different numbers of parameters and different training strategies, required only 3% of the memory and estimated 3% of the time of the leading pre-trained transformer-based model.  Our results demonstrate that efficient classification can be achieved with highly effective and affordable models.

To allow users to create music on their own terms, we're developing a tool that allows for free expression by removing limitations imposed by low-quality recordings and limited performance skills. To Dallinger's current all-encompassing approach, which focuses on a single genre, we're adopting a different angle. We're investigating the potential of transfer learning and neural audio synthesis to teach a performance model the genre of music it should generate, using separate datasets. We're starting our research by examining how well Dallinger's model generalizes across various prompts and investigating its internal representations. We're evaluating training the model on entire albums from multiple artists versus a single album from each artist to achieve better understanding of the model's internal representation of the music style, as well as the impact of including or excluding certain track characteristics in the training data.

Human-like animations of objects being thrown often feel more realistic than other methods, thanks to the natural variation seen in real-life throws and the animation techniques used. To achieve this realism, we've developed a model that takes into account the forces exerted during throwing motions and how different body parts contribute to the throw's strength. By analyzing forces from different body parts and speed variations in multiple frames, we can create a sense of the variation natural to throwing motions. A unique approach was used to generate trial motions and then refined under the set set constraints, along with a way to incorporate variation without altering average throw behavior. When compared to real-life footage, our results closely match the natural variation seen in throwing motions and perform well in controlled tests.

We introduce a syntax-aware attention model for neural machine translation that enables attention to focus on specific parts of input sentences. This technology facilitates translation of lengthy and structurally intricate sentences while offering control over translation fluency and word order. Our experiment involved multiple languages and revealed that adding syntax elements consistently had a positive effect on translation quality. Furthermore, our model's syntax-aware attention parameters were successfully transferred across languages to facilitate translation of low-resource languages.

We've developed and compared computational models that calculate snow lines in star-planet systems within their planetary discs. Our research focuses on how water snow data, which is often missing, affects the estimation of snow lines. We have created simplified models using the typical disc model, which allows us to account for different disc models and parameters, generating 10,000 sample models. Our sample shows significant variability, indicating that the water snow estimate is sensitive to multiple disc model parameters. Our sample reveals that the water snow estimate has high uncertainty, primarily due to the temperature range where water ice transitions to steam. When presented with actual disc data, our sample reveals the potential for the model to accurately predict the location of water snow lines. However, accurately measuring the water steam opacity in the model to align with observed data is essential for a precise prediction. Our sample further demonstrates that changing the water binding energy has a significant impact on the water snow lines, which needs to be considered in models.

We assess whether a predefined parameter set in a given model of discrete data provides a statistically significant fit to an observed empirical distribution. Our approach involves adjusting model parameters based on a target distribution, which is then fine-tuned by comparing it to the actual data. This process holds true for a variety of well-known distributions, including binomial, Poisson, and gamma, as well as their analogous discrete versions. Additionally, by utilizing kernel density estimation, our method can be expanded to cover complex data patterns, including those with multiple peaks.

This work presents an alternative to full quantum state learning, focusing instead on estimating specific expectation values. The approach leverages expectation values of powers and products of individual expectation values to construct hypermatrices that approximate the density matrix's diagonals. By leveraging convexity, the complexity of quantum state learning is significantly reduced, requiring optimization only over two parameters per diagonal element, thus making hypermatrix approximation efficient even for large quantum systems, including many-qubit states.

A novel approach to solving the Geometrical Optics inverse problem in two-dimensional, weakly heterogeneous media has been developed.  The method leverages two far-field measurements of a time-limited potential with support within a bounded domain.  The increased accuracy of a potential's construction can be attributed to refined asymptotic relations, derived from a time-extension principle initially presented in an author's previous study (2019).  The research includes a proof of the inverse problem's solvability and a forward asymptotic analysis, demonstrating the problem's sensitivity to high-frequency oscillations in the medium.  Additionally, the paper outlines a practical algorithm for reconstructing the time-limited potential with the ability to adapt to noisy data and adjust to the problem's dimensions.  The method's efficiency and stability have been validated through a reduced computational time requirement (by a factor of 100) and a lower error rate (by a factor of 1000) in comparison to a previous approach.  The algorithm's performance is further demonstrated through a direct application to a nonlinear problem and data data within noisy noise levels.  The method allows for a high-resolution potential reconstruction with an error of 0.0001 in two-dimensional data and an error of 0.001 in data with multiple dimensions.  The method's efficiency and stability are also demonstrated through a direct application to data with multiple dimensions and an additional computational cost of 0.001.

This paper compares two classes of class label transformation methods known as transmutations and mixture transformations, highlighting that the latter can be seen as limiting cases of the former. While focusing on continuous domains, we provide a unified framework for both approaches and derive key results using standard operations.

Linear regression with multiple related tasks is widely used in various machine learning applications, such as predicting linear trends, Bayesian analysis, and task-based tasks in computer vision. Recent research has highlighted the benefits of leveraging information from multiple related tasks to create more efficient algorithms. Our research develops new algorithms for solving linear regression with multiple related tasks that efficiently handle a broad spectrum of task relationships. The algorithms achieve optimal efficiency by adapting to different task relationships, and we achieve efficient results for various task relationships. Our findings demonstrate the effectiveness of adapting to related tasks and present efficient efficient algorithms for predicting tasks with linear trends.

We've observed that the effectiveness of post-training quantization oftenexceeds that of Knowledge Distillation when dealing with limited language resources.
Since Quantization inherently incorporates knowledge from the original model, wecan't simply combine its benefits with those from Knowledge Distillation, as adiosing information is a natural consequence of quantization.
To rectify this, we've developed a novel approach called 'Knowledge Distillation Quantization', a two-stage training process incorporating Knowledge Distillation after quantization, ultimately surpassing the individual benefits of both techniques and yielding better results on low-resource languages.
Moreover, our approach surpasses the previously best-known results achieved through Fine-tuning with quantization.

We discuss the known upper and lower bounds for the Turán density of $unicycle edges$ in $k$-uniform graphs for various values of $k$, building on work by Baber and Talbot (J. Combin. Theory Ser. B 134 (2018) 100-114) who reported a lower bound of $1-\frac{1}{e}$ (approximately $0.368$) and specifically $1-\frac{1}{e}+\varepsilon$ for large $k$. We provide a general upper bound of approximately $0.371$, along with more precise values of $0.3685+$ for quadrang-free edges in quartic graphs and $0.3683-$ for tricycles in triplicates. We introduce a new model-independent approach based on the spectral properties of the random hypergraph's normalized adjacency tensor, anchored in the central limit theorem, that may benefit a wide range of problems. Our method relies on a novel, general approach to count specific subgraphs (such as cycles and trees) in random hypergraphs, utilizing new and existing formulas. Our work extends a previous finding by Feige, and specifically shows the emergence of a unique "unicycle" structure in random bipartite graphs, as well as the absence of multi-cycle structures, in the bipartite and directed versions of the random graph.

Our research focuses on addressing the challenge of data scarcity in developing robust deep learning models for clinical applications, such as disease detection. The proposed solution involves introducing an unsupervised framework that uses pseudo-labels generated from high-confidence regions in images to label augmented data. These pseudo-labels are determined by the highest class probabilities predicted by a model. The labelled data is then used to train a model that is subsequently applied to the original images to create pseudo-labels for categorizing positive examples. Our model generates a confidence map that identifies the most reliable labels through the application of filters, which are then used to label corresponding images. These newly labelled data are used to create a model that is iteratively improved by exposing it to different image augmentations. Our model was tested on a dataset containing non-infectious COVID-19 pneumonia, with a sensitivity of 0.90 and a specificity of 0.87 when using a 10% requirement for labelled data.

In recent years, researchers have been focusing on developing vision-language models that integrate both vision and language understanding capabilities. These models excel at various vision-language tasks and are becoming the go-to choice. However, they are often limited by the need for extensive, high-quality datasets and time-consuming processes like weakly-supervised segmentation and 3D reconstruction to create high-quality training data. To address these issues, we're taking a different approach by incorporating prompt learning into an image captioning framework to create more precise visual descriptions, which can then be used for other vision-language tasks without requiring large datasets. By exploring this direction, we've developed two versions of the method - one using a pre-trained language model either with random initialisation or optimization, and another utilizing a VLM with a guided optimization algorithm based on the VLM's own knowledge. These alternatives demonstrate the effectiveness of prompt learning in this context and showcase its versatility and adaptability across various vision-language tasks.

 situations where one advantage does not completely negate another disadvantage.

This research focuses on developing strong speech-to-speech speech translation systems that can operate without extensive training data. The objective is to create models with superior generalization capabilities using a significant amount of parallel speech-text pairs and a small number of limited datasets. The proposed techniques leverage the relationships between languages, speeches, and text, and combine multiple amounts of pre-trained knowledge to create robust representations. The novel approaches outperform current best practices on all tested settings. The results indicate that language models can effectively be used for zero-shot speech translation and that speech representation can be optimized through the combination of multiple pre-trained models. The proposed methods show the most promising results for achieving zero-shot speech translation.

The paper explores the application of the fading memory idea to derive heat conduction equations for both simple and anisotropic materials under both local and non-local conditions. It introduces a general approach for simple materials based on memory density and one for anisotropic materials based on memory tensor density. Derivations of heat flux equations for various constitutive models, including those by Fick, Fourier, Cattaneo, and Duffin, are explored within non-local frameworks. For tensors, a general invariance principle is proposed, ensuring that a constitutive equation remains invariant under coordinate transformations. This leads to a general representation theorem that allows for the determination of the memory tensor for symmetric materials based on a star domain, a Cauchy neighborhood, and a tensor of identity.

To effectively manage the growing energy demand, particularly during peak periods, it is essential to accurately forecast and prepare for these peaks in advance. Previous studies have primarily focused on total energy demand, neglecting the unique characteristics of peak demand. This paper proposes a novel approach that fuses conventional energy demand forecasts with specific peak time predictions, resulting in significant improvements in forecasting accuracy. By incorporating known peak times and a recognition of forecasting uncertainties, this method outperforms traditional methods, showing a notable 20% improvement in accuracy during peak times. Furthermore, this approach can enable grid operators to more efficiently schedule peak power plants, reducing the unmet energy demand and enhancing overall energy supply reliability.

Machine learning algorithms can swiftly adapt to shifting environments and answer complex questions, but their rapid learning often leads to inaccuracies and errors, especially when learning from limited data. By integrating subject matter expertise, we enhance the learning process and improve AI model's inferences and predictions. We introduce a new method called Knowledge-based Learning (K2L) that combines machine learning and human knowledge, allowing the model to learn from faulty information as well. Our initial findings indicate that incorporating human knowledge significantly boosts the performance of our proposed framework.

Many medical imaging analysis applications require precise lesion detection, but this is a challenging task, especially when it involves training deep convolutional neural networks. This difficulty is due to the need for detailed image annotation, which is time-consuming and expensive in medical imaging. This work presents a novel, data-driven framework that relies solely on image- level labels, making it applicable to various imaging modalities without needing detailed annotation protocols. This is achieved by first designing a loss function that converts image-level labels into pixel-level segmentation, then leveraging the combination of pre-trained deep learning features and advanced image processing techniques to achieve accurate segmentation using significantly fewer data (around 100 images). We demonstrate the method's effectiveness with real-world data from two lung cancer screening projects, showing that it requires a 10-fold reduction in the number of training images, while delivering high performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods.

Automatically locating and grading vertebrae in spinal X-rays is a crucial first step in developing computer-aided spinal disease diagnosis systems. Semi-supervised deep learning models have shown promising results in this area by significantly reducing the manual annotation requirements. Nevertheless, existing semi-supervised models often fail to achieve optimal identification rates due to their inability to effectively pinpoint the minor geometric variations between consecutive vertebrae. In this study, we introduce an innovative approach that leverages a multi-scale deep learning model to automatically detect and segment vertebrae, followed by an instance matching process to accurately identify their positions. Moreover, our model exploits minor geometric variations to enhance the accuracy of vertebrae identification, thereby improving overall performance. Extensive experiments conducted on a comprehensive spinal X-ray dataset demonstrate that our proposed model surpasses state-of-the-art models by a substantial margin of 5.56% in identification rate, with only a minimal time overhead of 1.03 seconds per X-ray image.

To enhance the research on light-matter interaction within low-density electromagnetic fields, our study investigates fundamental properties of states involving light and matter in an optical cavity experiment using Rb atoms and a specific configuration involving standing waves and a specific band structure Rb5s state rotation. We increase stability by enhancing vacuum fluctuations affecting the Rb5s state, achieved through reducing the cavity spacing, resulting in improved signal and reduced noise. This improvement is quantified and correlated with theoretical predictions, showing the Rb5s state decay rate increases with the reduction in cavity spacing. Our study demonstrates that integrating high-density Rb atoms with microcavity structures can potentially enhance the production of polariton states involving light, matter, and electronic vacuum fluctuations using a Rb state configuration and standing wave setup.

Recent breakthroughs in spring-based actuation continue to spark interest due to their potential for innovative legged locomotion, a field in which they excel. The unique combination of actuators, controllers, and other system elements is the key to their success, and further optimization is an area of active research. The specific design of these actuators significantly impacts their performance, and here we introduce a novel method to optimize a critical component of the system - the actuator's internal design. The approach is versatile and can be applied to existing actuator types to improve their performance in various tasks. The method is demonstrated through the optimization of a compliant serial elastic actuator for a legged robot's push-up movement, and our findings highlight substantial gains in both energy efficiency and mechanical power output.

Determining whether a quantum state has real, negative or complex components is a significant problem with significant implications for various applications. Although existing methods for solving this problem require exponentially increasing resources, we found a way to determine the nature of a quantum state using an intermediate-scale noisy quantum device. We established a method based on random unitary measurements that can accurately classify quantum states, and tested our approach with different types of quantum simulators, including digital and gate-based devices. Our findings demonstrate that noisy quantum devices can effectively determine the separability of quantum states, even in simulated environments with gate limitations.

Using the PENCIL CODE, we investigated the fine-scale tearing parity instability through numerical simulations. We investigated how electron drift kinetic instability and its reconnection process are influenced by electron effects in different guide field strengths and kinetic plasma parameters. Specifically, we explored the effects of the guided field using three different beta values (0.01, 0.1, and 1) and three different kinetic plasma parameters ($m_e/m_i$) in three different cases: 1/100, 1/1000, and 1/10000. From our 9 different case studies, we observed that all our simulations satisfy the necessary condition for kinetic tearing instability. However, due to the influence of the guided field and electron effects, the characteristics of the tearing mode are significantly altered. For instance, the disturbed areas and oscillations seen in the guided field and total pressure profiles are caused by the combined effects of the electron displacement and kinetic tearing. Additionally, it's observed that the mode changes from being even to odd parity, which is attributed to the combined influence of guide field and kinetic effects. Furthermore, it's observed that the even mode exhibits less disturbance in the guided field, but the kinetic effects lead to significant fluctuations in the guided field.

Our understanding of image semantics relies heavily on recognizing fashion items, despite the limited success of fashion instance-level image retrieval, due to a lack of comprehensive fashion datasets that provide rich semantic information. To bridge this gap, our study proposes a new approach called fashion semantic retrieval, which involves finding similar target fashion images based on given semantic descriptions. We introduce a novel fashion semantic retrieval dataset called Fashion2Sem, along with a fashion semantic embedding model that can be trained end-to-end. To accommodate a wide range of applications, we designed a flexible retrieval framework called RSRS that supports both semantic and fashion semantic scenarios, and can be employed with a large and diverse collection of conventional fashion retrieval datasets. Our proposed method achieves impressive state-of-the-art results on both fashion semantic and traditional fashion retrieval tasks. The our code and datasets are publicly available on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/zhiliu1208/Fashion2Sem.

In this research, we investigate how solutions to ill-posed problems can be approximated using gradient flow methods. We demonstrate that selecting an optimal stopping time is crucial in achieving accurate results. Consequently, we examine various regularization techniques for transient nonlinear problems and validate our approaches through numerical experiments on models such as the Cahn-Hilliard equation and the Helfrich energy functional.

We resolve the all-pixel pixel correspondence challenge in monocular depth estimation by introducing the first cost constructor capable of handling occlusions and generatingOcculiant depth values that accurately reflect actual depths. Our innovative constructor accurately maps input images to depth values with unprecedented precision across diverse datasets and architectures, including established cost constructors, cutting-edge diffusion models, and advanced neural geometric rendering methods.

The Fokas-Lenells equation and its connection to the A(1), D(1) principal bundle framework are examined in this study.  It is discovered that the specific geometric configurations of a two-dimensional massive Thirring model and the U(1) principal bundle are closely related to the solutions and symmetries of the Fokas-Lenells equation.  These findings shed light on the interplay between integrable nonlinear differential equations and global gauge theories.

In our double field theory framework, we have constructed and examined the equations of motion for both gravity and gauge theories with different spacetime symmetries. These equations are derived from a simple action that maintains spacetime general covariance. The resulting spacetime equations and level-trace constraints lead to additional physical and mathematical implications such as a specific self-consistency condition. We have further investigated these symplectic conditions and general covariance in more detail. Our action formulation for non-Riemannian gravities can also be used as a starting point to develop equations of motion for even more complex theories of gravity.

In recent years, the number of Home WiFi networks that support IoT devices has significantly increased due to growing demand for IoT applications. As a result, IoT Home WiFi networks have seen a rise in traffic, leading to substantial issues with delay. To address this, IoT Home WiFi association methods have been developed to improve performance by considering various metrics, such as channel load awareness and device QoS requirements. However, existing approaches have overlooked a crucial aspect - the availability of available channel bandwidth. To fill this gap, a new association framework has been developed that enables IoT devices to choose their preferred Home WiFi access point based on the channel aware method. Through extensive simulations, the proposed channel aware association outperforms traditional association methods that rely on signal strength, resulting in improved average goodput (7.6% improvement) and reduced average delay (15.6% improvement) in a challenging scenario.
